posts.title: Math, faster
posts.author: ASKA Research
posts.summary: OpenAI published 722 machine-written mathematics manuscripts in 372 result families on 2026-10-06; ASKA read the corpus on day one, ranked the headline claims and checked the evidence behind each. Nothing was independently confirmed, a minority had machine-checked proofs, and the real shift is that checking, not discovering, is now the bottleneck.
posts.relevance: Archetypal Foundation0 entry: AI-driven frontier progress whose truth depends on human plus machine (Lean) verification; supplies the claimed / machine-checked / reviewed / withdrawn vocabulary for the whole tracker.

posts.title: Crypto Industry Lowdown
posts.author: ASKA Research
posts.summary: A guide for readers returning to crypto: prices fell, but stablecoins, ETFs, custody, perpetuals and agent-payment rails became infrastructure. The security threat moved from contract code to keys and suppliers.
posts.relevance: Low-medium: AI agents as economic actors (x402, ERC-8004, ERC-8183) and AI-assisted auditing, with the caveat that AI finds code bugs but does not fix key custody. Not investment advice.

posts.title: Post-Training Your Own Models
posts.author: ASKA Research
posts.summary: A practical guide to teaching an open-weight model a task, a workflow or your writing voice: methods, memory math, prices, tools, evaluation and three playbooks. Its first rule is to try a better prompt, then retrieval, and only then training.
posts.relevance: Medium-high: puts lab-grade model customization within reach of one person and one GPU, which is Foundation0's 'instruments for independent researchers' pillar.

posts.title: The Naming Decides Who Will Run the Machines
posts.author: The ASKA Team
posts.summary: ASKA's IR-Taxonomy gives non-engineers five plain names for agentic systems, so a buyer knows what kind of machine they own before a demo decides for them. Each name comes with one question the owner is entitled to have answered in writing.
posts.relevance: High for symbiosis: a shared plain-language vocabulary keeps humans accountable for the machines they deploy.

posts.title: Subtractive Fragility
posts.author: ASKA Research
posts.summary: Long calm periods make systems fragile less by piling up risk than by quietly removing capacities that only pay off in a crisis. Those capacities get rebuilt only when someone can bill for the rebuild; the essay makes seven dated, falsifiable predictions (2027–2035).
posts.relevance: High: AI capex is physically an electrification cycle; Prediction 7 (a senior-expertise shortage from untrained juniors) is a precise symbiosis risk; the design law is a funding model for a lasting public-benefit foundation; dated, falsifiable predictions echo Seldon's crises.

posts.title: Prediction Market Outlook
posts.author: ASKA Research
posts.summary: A snapshot of what public prediction markets priced on 2026-09-08, read as scenario weights rather than forecasts. Includes a small regression on what makes a market's probability lopsided.
posts.relevance: Low: a model of stated limits (n = 23, selection bias), plus one AI-policy signal (US–China AI agreement 10%). Dated and client-addressed.

posts.title: The Agents Are Replaceable. The Operating System Is Not.
posts.author: The ASKA Team
posts.summary: A one-person consultancy runs like a ten-person firm on a team of AI agents. The agents are interchangeable; what makes the system work is the discipline around them: handoffs, blocking gates, checks on the real output, and memory written down outside any one session.
posts.relevance: Very high: ASKA's working example of biological and digital intelligence cooperating under explicit rules, with an honest limit ('asserts value; it does not yet demonstrate it').

posts.title: The Institution Is the Bottleneck
posts.author: ASKA Research
posts.summary: Healthcare, education and government keep failing to adopt working technologies in the same way. A technology takes on the incentives of the institution it lands in, so it sticks only where an outcome has an owner, a measure and a priced consequence.
posts.relevance: High for the public-good pillar: explains why free AI tools (e.g. medcode, nutrak) need an owner, a measure and a channel, not just good software.

posts.title: The Money Skips the Public Good
posts.author: ASKA Research
posts.summary: Canada's 'AI for All' strategy names the public, but every funding channel it built pays only for AI that can bill for its own value. Public-good AI is left with the slow, constrained charitable route, so the legal form chosen on day one decides whether the mission survives.
posts.relevance: Very high: directly about how a public-benefit AI organization (a 'Foundation') and its free apps should be structured and funded.

posts.title: No Coup, Just Comfort
posts.author: ASKA Research
posts.summary: Decentralized systems are rarely defeated by enemies; they are given away one convenient default at a time. The industry cannot see it because its metrics count what adoption adds and nothing that decentralization loses.
posts.relevance: Medium: the same drift from help to habit to dependence threatens human–AI partnership; 'measure what is being subtracted' is a design principle for Foundation0.
